challenges.name: monolith-or-microservices-evidence
challenges.title: Monolith or Microservices? Read the evidence
challenges.description: RFC-031 proposes splitting the CodeDev platform into seven microservices, and its first step has already sent receipts for declined cards. Six statements on one evidence pack - the team map (A), the deploy pipeline (B), the traffic profile (C), the proposal (D) and the INC-77 trace (E) - take you from reading the evidence past two wrong explanations to a hypothesis, a decision and its verification.

questions.question:
Evidence A - team and ownership (CODEOWNERS, repository codedev-platform, one deployable app):
/src/modules/catalog/         @codedev/platform-team
/src/modules/orders/          @codedev/platform-team
/src/modules/payments/        @codedev/platform-team
/src/modules/notifications/   @codedev/platform-team
/src/modules/progress/        @codedev/platform-team
# platform-team: 6 developers, one sprint board, one on-call rotation
# One Postgres database. Code that reads the orders table:
#   src/modules/orders/, src/modules/payments/, src/modules/progress/report.ts

Evidence B - deploy pipeline, last 30 days:
Pipeline deploy-production: 19 runs, 17 succeeded, 2 failed, median 20m 10s
Median step durations
  install dependencies          1m 40s
  lint + typecheck              2m 05s
  test (unit + integration)    12m 30s   1 worker, test files run one after another
  build                         1m 55s
  migrate database              0m 40s
  rollout (2 instances)         1m 20s
Failed runs
  2026-09-30  rollout  health check failed in src/modules/progress/report.ts:
              ERROR: column o.amount does not exist
              (migration 0412 renamed orders.amount to orders.amount_vnd) - rolled back
  2026-10-03  migrate  ERROR: canceling statement due to lock timeout
              (migration 0412b on orders waited behind checkout transactions, lock_timeout 5s)

Statement: "Both failed deploys last month came from one change to the orders table, a table that code in three modules reads directly."
questions.explanation: True. In B the first failure is the rename in migration 0412 breaking a query in src/modules/progress/report.ts, and the second is the reworked migration 0412b on the same orders table waiting behind checkout transactions. A lists orders, payments and progress/report.ts as code that reads orders directly. So the deploy failures come from a table shared by several modules, not from the amount of code in one deployable. The common misconception is to read every failed deploy as proof that "the monolith is too big"; the evidence points at shared data, which a split does not remove unless the data is split too.

Evidence D - RFC-031 "Split the platform into microservices":
Services (7): catalog, orders, payments, notifications, progress, users, leaderboard
Each service: own repository, own pipeline, own database; HTTP calls and events between them
Expected benefits: "deploys get fast because each service is small",
                   "catalog can scale on its own",
                   "a bug in one service cannot break the others"

Statement: "Splitting the app into the seven services of RFC-031 would by itself bring deploys well under 20 minutes, because each service would deploy less code."
questions.explanation: False. B shows that 12m 30s of the 20 minutes is the test step running on one worker. Seven pipelines would each still install, lint, test, build and roll out, and nothing in the RFC changes how tests run. The direct fix for this evidence is to run tests in parallel and, on pull requests, only the tests of the changed modules, which works in one repository today. The misconception is that deploy time grows with the size of the codebase; it grows with the slowest step, and you find that step in the pipeline, not in the architecture diagram.

questions.question:
Evidence C - traffic profile, last 4 weeks:
Route group          avg req/min   Mon 19:00-21:00 req/min   p95
GET  /catalog/*         2,400            9,800                 85 ms
GET  /progress/*          600            2,100                 60 ms
POST /orders               48              190                310 ms
Catalog: about 50 reads for every write (writes are admin edits)
App: 2 instances x 2 vCPU, CPU average 22%, peak 71% (Mondays 19:00-21:00)
Postgres: CPU peak 38%

Evidence D - RFC-031 "Split the platform into microservices":
Services (7): catalog, orders, payments, notifications, progress, users, leaderboard
Each service: own repository, own pipeline, own database; HTTP calls and events between them
Expected benefits: "deploys get fast because each service is small",
                   "catalog can scale on its own",
                   "a bug in one service cannot break the others"

Statement: "The Monday evening spike shows that the catalog needs its own service so that it can scale independently."
questions.explanation: False. At the peak the app uses 71% CPU on two instances with 2 vCPU each, and Postgres 38%: nothing is saturated. A third instance of the whole app during the Monday window, or caching catalog pages that are read about 50 times for every write, covers the spike for far less than a new service with its own pipeline, database and on-call. Independent scaling pays when one part needs very different resources from the rest, or scaling the whole app becomes expensive; C shows neither. The misconception is "there is a spike, so split the part with the spike" without a number that says the whole app cannot absorb it.

questions.question:
Evidence E - INC-77, two days after "extract notifications" was merged:
37 receipts sent for declined payments, 12 learners got course access without paying
Trace of one checkout (order o_51873)
10:14:02.104  orders         placeOrder o_51873 course=redis-patterns amount=149000
10:14:02.106  orders         email.sendReceipt -> POST notifications/receipts o_51873
10:14:02.131  notifications  receipt queued for hoa.tran@example.com o_51873
10:14:02.133  orders         events.publish order.paid o_51873
10:14:02.140  progress       grantAccess u_9310 redis-patterns (consumer of order.paid)
10:14:02.902  orders         payments.charge o_51873 -> declined (insufficient_funds)
10:14:02.910  orders         orders.save o_51873 payment_failed
PR #611, first hunk of placeOrder:
+    // notifications is its own service now: tell it as early as possible
+    deps.email.sendReceipt(order.learnerEmail, order.id, order.amountVnd);
+    deps.events.publish("order.paid", { orderId: order.id, learnerId: order.learnerId, courseId: order.courseId });
     const result = deps.payments.charge(order.id, order.amountVnd);

Statement: "The receipts went out for declined cards because placeOrder sends the receipt and publishes order.paid before it calls charge; the same code would do the same with notifications still a module in the same process."
questions.explanation: True. The trace shows the sending side's own order: sendReceipt at .106, publish order.paid at .133, charge at .902. Nothing was reordered by the network; orders sent the side effects first, and the diff shows the lines that moved them there. The extraction was the motive ("tell it as early as possible") but not the mechanism: an in-process EmailSender called first would send the same wrong receipt, and an in-process progress module listening for order.paid would grant the same access. The misconception is to blame distribution or eventual consistency for a bug that is plain call order in one function.

Statement: "For this team, keeping one deployable app with enforced module boundaries, plus written triggers that would reopen the decision, fits the evidence better than the seven-service plan."
questions.explanation: True. A shows one team of six owning every module, so separate services would not give separate teams independent deploys; B points to a serial test step and a shared table, both fixable directly; C shows spare capacity; E shows that the first extraction added a failure across three modules. A modular monolith makes the boundaries real now (public API per module, one owner per table, one-way dependencies) and keeps the option to extract a module later. The triggers - a second team, a module blocked from deploying, a module that needs very different scaling, repeated failures crossing modules - say when to look again. The misconception is that "monolith" means "no structure", or that the decision is made once and forever.

Statement: "A test that runs one successful checkout and asserts that exactly one receipt is sent proves that INC-77 is fixed."
questions.explanation: False. The code from PR #611 also sends exactly one receipt for a successful checkout, so that test passes before and after the fix and cannot tell them apart. INC-77 is about declined payments: the test must run a declined checkout and a gateway timeout and assert that no receipt and no order.paid event are sent, and assert the call order for a paid order: charge, save as paid, receipt, event. In production, a query for receipts whose order is not paid should return the 37 rows before the deploy and none after it. The misconception is to test the happy path, which the incident never broke.

challenges.name: receipt-before-payment
challenges.title: Receipt Before Payment
challenges.description: Two days after the notifications module of CodeDev was extracted into its own service, learners report receipts for cards that were declined, and some of them can open courses they never paid for, because the progress module grants access when it sees an "order.paid" event. placeOrder(order, deps) uses four ports: PaymentGateway.charge, OrderRepository.save, EmailSender.sendReceipt and EventBus.publish. Fix it so that a valid order is charged first; when the charge succeeds, the order is saved as "paid" with its charge id and only then the receipt is sent and "order.paid" is published (result "paid"); a declined charge saves "payment_failed" and a gateway timeout saves "payment_unknown", and neither sends a receipt or publishes an event. Invalid orders (amount not a positive integer, email without "@") stay "rejected" with no port called. Input: a JSON list of checkouts { order, payment }, where payment ("succeeded", "declined" or "timeout") scripts the fake gateway. Output: for up to 10 checkouts the call log of the fakes and the result of each, then a summary line with the counts of results, receipts, events and side effects sent before the order was saved as paid; for more than 10 checkouts only the summary line.
hints: A receipt tells the learner "you paid" and order.paid tells progress "grant access". At the moment placeOrder sends them, what does it know about the payment?
Run a declined checkout and read the call log from top to bottom: which lines appear before payments.charge? Then compare the three answers of the gateway: which of them make the order paid?

A similar case on other data: a password-reset flow that emails "your password was changed" and then calls users.updatePassword, which can fail validation. The safe order is update, check that it worked, save, and only then email; a failed update sends nothing.
